title: Let my people go (Exodus 5–10)
hook: bricks without straw, then plagues against a hardened heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, who am I: five excuses at the burning bush, and one answer under all of them. Your line was I will be with thee. Did you take the step? Today closes a week that ran from Joseph's tears through the midwives, the basket and the bush. Day three hundred seventy-one.

Moses and Aaron walk into Pharaoh's court and say four words. "Let my people go." Enslaved people in America would later sing them in the spiritual Go Down, Moses. And Pharaoh's answer is a shrug: who is this Lord, that I should listen to him? I don't know him. Then he does something any overworked employee would recognize. He doesn't argue. He raises the quota. Same number of bricks every day, he orders, but you won't be given straw anymore. Go find your own.
screen: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.` → `WHO IS THIS LORD?` → `SAME BRICKS, NO STRAW.`

segments.voice: First, the bricks. The Hebrews scatter across Egypt gathering stubble, and of course they can't make the count. So the Egyptian taskmasters beat the Hebrew foremen. The foremen go to Pharaoh and get nowhere, and on the way out they turn on Moses: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses turns to God: why did you ever send me? Things got worse the moment I spoke. Second, the plagues. Blood in the Nile. Frogs everywhere. Gnats. Flies. Sickness on the cattle. Boils. Hail. Locusts. Then darkness so thick it can be felt. Nine in these chapters; the tenth comes tomorrow. Pharaoh's magicians copy the first ones, then give up at the gnats and tell him: this is the finger of God. Third, the hard heart. Over and over Pharaoh promises to let the people go, then changes his mind when the trouble lifts. Sometimes the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Elsewhere it says God hardened it. Readers have long wrestled with that. Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas taught that God doesn't put evil into anyone; when God is said to harden a heart, it means God withholds grace from someone who has already chosen to refuse it. Fourth, the cry. This is a story about bricks and wages and bodies, not only souls. The Catechism lists cheating workers of their wages among the sins that cry out to heaven, and Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a whole letter, Rerum Novarum, on the rights of workers. That teaching leans on stories like this one: God hearing the cry of people forced to work without straw.
screen: `BRICKS WITHOUT STRAW.` · `NINE PLAGUES, AND THE FINGER OF GOD.` · `A HEART THAT KEEPS HARDENING.` · `A CRY THAT REACHES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember workers treated unjustly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen, sewed the shirt you're wearing, cleans the building you work in, drives the truck that brought your packages. Some of them are paid fairly. Some are making bricks without straw. Let one face come to mind, even an imagined one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name or by work, using Moses's words: let my people go. If you don't, just hold them in mind with respect for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Let my people go. God's demand to Pharaoh through Moses, answered with heavier work and a heart that kept hardening. Today's word.
Your line: let my people go. Today, look up who makes one thing you use every day, and thank one worker you'd usually walk past. Day three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholic social teaching, beginning with Pope Leo XIII's letter Rerum Novarum in 1891, defends workers' right to a just wage, and the Catechism lists defrauding laborers of their wages among the sins that cry to heaven.

fork.setup: you're Pharaoh. Moses and Aaron just told you their God says let my people go. what's your move?
options: let them go for a few days to worship.
keep the brick quota and take away their straw.
fork.reveal: he doesn't argue. he makes the work harder: same number of bricks, and they gather their own straw.

original.note: Hebrew: send out my people, let them go. the demand returns again and again through the plagues.

trapdoor: what you thought: a movie scene with special effects.
what it means: a story of forced labor, a God who hears the workers' cry, and a ruler whose heart keeps hardening.
what a scholar hears: more than one Hebrew verb hardens the heart, chazaq and kaved among them, and the text says both that Pharaoh hardened himself and that God hardened him.

sources.ref: Augustine; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 79, a. 3

notes: Week-end look-back (365–371) is carried in the review: Joseph's tears, the midwives, the basket, the bush.
Go Down, Moses: African American spiritual (19th century), public domain; only its refrain is referenced. Confirm the framing.
Plague list (7–10): blood, frogs, gnats (DR 'sciniphs'), flies, livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness; the magicians' 'finger of God' at 8:19 (DR 8:19 / Hebrew 8:15). Confirm verse numbering.

Pharaoh hardens his own heart (e.g., 8:15, 8:32) and God hardens it (9:12; 10:20, 27). Aquinas ST I-II q.79 a.3 (God as cause of spiritual blindness and hardness by withholding grace); Augustine similarly. Confirm the summary.
CCC 1867 lists 'injustice to the wage earner' among sins that cry to heaven; CCC 2434 on just wages. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'singing ever since' and 'every bad boss in history' sweeping claims; 'later it says God hardened' changed to 'elsewhere' (God announces the hardening already at 4:21 and 7:3); sins-that-cry-to-heaven attributed to the Catechism; fork no longer calls Moses and Aaron 'two shepherds'; trapdoor no longer says there are exactly two hardening verbs (qashah at 7:3 is a third) or that the text moves in one direction.
